description: PDF-derived Markdown of the public August 2025 City of Richfield, Minnesota stormwater model update and flood-risk prioritization study, drafted into an eight-section Minnesota DNR Flood Hazard Mitigation application, then verified and edited.

source.provenance: Mistral OCR (mistral-ocr-latest) of the public Barr Engineering report, assembled with CityCatalyst page-marker, header/footer, and table rules. The certifying engineer, licence number, and private email correspondents are redacted.

facts.statement: The stormwater model covers the entire City of Richfield and the adjacent areas that drain into Richfield.

evidence.text: The model covers the entire city and the areas of adjacent cities that drain into Richfield.

facts.statement: Barr updated the PCSWMM model with LiDAR data collected in 2022 and published by the USGS.

evidence.text: Barr updated the existing PCSWMM model to incorporate the Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data collected in 2022 and published by the United States Geological Survey (USGS)

facts.statement: The updated model simulates four design storm events, including the climate-adaptation MCE100-year event, using the MSE3 rainfall distribution.

evidence.text: The four design storm events use the Midwest Southeast 3 (MSE3) rainfall distribution
The PCSWMM model was used to simulate four design rainfall events.

facts.statement: Flood-risk areas were scored on storm system conditions, critical infrastructure, frequency of flooding, social vulnerability index, and number of flood-prone structures.

evidence.text:
The criteria selected to score the flood-risk areas are:

- Storm system conditions
- Critical infrastructure
- Frequency of flooding
- Social vulnerability index (SVI)
- Number of flood-prone structures

facts.statement: 746 flood-risk areas were evaluated, 601 of them within or primarily within the municipal boundary.

evidence.text: A total of 746 flood-risk areas were evaluated from the study area with 601 flood-risk areas located within or primarily within the municipal boundary.

facts.statement: The city selected three flood-risk areas, for which six mitigation concepts were identified and evaluated in the updated model.

evidence.text: Three flood-risk areas were selected by the city based on the project prioritization framework developed. For these three flood-risk areas a total of six mitigation concepts were identified and evaluated in the updated stormwater model.

facts.statement: The selected flood-risk areas are near Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace.

evidence.text: The area around Wilson Pond is one of the locations with the largest risk of flooding in the city.
For these reasons the city selected this area to evaluate concepts for system modifications to reduce flood risk.
The flood-risk area Northwest of Roosevelt Park was selected by the city for further evaluation.
The flood-risk area near Woodlawn Terrace was selected by the city for further evaluation.

facts.statement: The model study area is approximately 8.8 square miles.

evidence.text: The model study area covers the total watershed area included in the H&H model which is approximately 8.8 square miles

facts.statement: At Wilson Pond the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year 24-hour rainfall event.

evidence.text: The area around Wilson Pond is one of the locations with the largest risk of flooding in the city. This area impacts the most residential structures in a single location, the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year 24-hour rainfall event

facts.statement: Surface storage and underground storage near Wilson Pond were ruled out because of space and shallow groundwater.

evidence.text: Options that were considered but not pursued for the area near Wilson Pond include adding surface storage areas, underground storage, and a pump to lower the water level in Wilson Pond ahead of a storm event. Surface storage was not considered due to a lack of undeveloped space near the flood-risk area and the city's direction to not consider property acquisition for flood-risk reduction. Underground storage was not considered due to the expected shallow groundwater in the area.

facts.statement: The selected areas lie in parts of the city with a high social vulnerability index.

evidence.text: Wilson Pond is located within an area of the city with a high social vulnerability index

The flood-risk area Northwest of Roosevelt Park was selected by the city for further evaluation. This flood-risk area impacts multiple structures in a single location, the lowest structures are affected during the 10-year 24-hour duration rainfall event, the flood-risk area is located within an area of the city with a high social vulnerability index

The flood-risk area near Woodlawn Terrace was selected by the city for further evaluation. This flood-risk area impacts multiple structures in a single location, the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year 24-hour duration rainfall event, the storm sewer pipes are classified as moderate to high risk, the flood-risk area is located within an area of the city with a high social vulnerability index

facts.statement: The applicant is the City of Richfield, Minnesota.
The application targets the Minnesota DNR Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program.
Richfield has a recorded population of 36,994.
746 flood-risk areas were evaluated, 601 within or primarily within the municipal boundary.
Flood-risk areas were prioritized on storm system conditions, critical infrastructure, frequency of flooding, social vulnerability index, and number of flood-prone structures.
The project addresses the flood-risk areas near Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace.
The city selected three flood-risk areas, for which six mitigation concepts were identified and evaluated in the updated stormwater model.
At Wilson Pond the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year 24-hour rainfall event.
The evaluated projects, their model results and their cost estimates are concept-level designs with planning-level cost estimates.
The concept cost estimates are carried into the funding or financing sections.
Costs are stated in 2025 US dollars.
The report states a -30% to +50% accuracy range for its estimates.
Surface storage and underground storage near Wilson Pond were ruled out because of space and shallow groundwater.
The selected areas lie in parts of the city with a high social vulnerability index.
Table 5-7 lists Woodlawn Terrace Concept A at $1,540,000 with an upper estimate of $2,695,000, above the table note's stated +50% range.

Surface storage near Wilson Pond was not pursued because of limited undeveloped space.
The prioritization incorporated the social vulnerability index.
746 flood-risk areas were evaluated, 601 of them within or primarily within the Richfield municipal boundary.
The alternatives were modeled against 2-, 10- and 100-year, 24-hour design storms.

Every concept's modeled 10-year, 24-hour peak water-level reductions are still stated: Wilson Pond Concept A 1.4, 0.8 and 3.9 feet; Concept B 0.6, 0.4 and 1.9 feet; Concept C 0.6, 0.5 and 2.3 feet; northwest of Roosevelt Park 3.7, 1.0 and 0.5 feet; near Woodlawn Terrace Concept A 0.1 and 0.1 foot; and Concept B 0.8 and 0.5 foot.
Wilson Pond Concept B uses a 5-foot-by-5-foot box culvert and Concept C two parallel 5-foot-by-5-foot box culverts from Wilson Pond to Highway 494.
The cost estimates exclude planning, engineering and design; construction management; permitting; property or easement acquisition; operations and maintenance; and monitoring.
The modeled results are planning-level outcomes, not final design commitments.
At Wilson Pond, underground storage was not pursued because shallow groundwater is expected, and pumped drawdown was not pursued because of the high flow rate needed within an assumed 24-hour period.

Northwest of Roosevelt Park, surface storage was not pursued because the open space is higher than the flood-risk area and increased downstream capacity was not evaluated further because the area drains to Norby's Pond; near Woodlawn Terrace, surface storage was not pursued because the open space is developed with baseball fields and parking lots.

Wilson Pond concepts would increase the volume and peak rate of discharge leaving Richfield and need coordination with the City of Bloomington or MnDOT; the near Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage concept needs an agreement with the parking-lot owner.
No survey data was collected to verify whether the identified structures are flood-prone.
The Woodlawn Terrace area affects three high-density housing structures.

All eight [Information needed: ...] questions are still asked: selected location and concept, selection rationale, environmental effects, social and economic effects, public input, environmental review status, water-plan alignment, and wetland replacement credits.
The concept note is unchanged; no authorized agent is invented.
